Can you explain the main options in simple terms?
Absolutely! Here's a simple breakdown of the main spirit categories:
Whiskey — The umbrella term for spirits made from grains and aged in barrels. We offer over 20,000 spirits including Scotch, Bourbon, Rye, and more.
Bourbon — American whiskey made with at least 51% corn, giving it a sweet, warm flavor with notes of vanilla, caramel, and spice. It's aged in new charred oak barrels, which gives it that signature amber color.
Scotch — Whisky made in Scotland (note the spelling without the 'e'). It tends to be smoother and sometimes smokier than bourbon, with a wide range of flavors depending on the region.
Rye — Whiskey made primarily from rye grain, giving it a spicier, drier taste compared to bourbon's sweetness.
Tequila — Made from blue agave in Mexico. Ranges from clear and crisp (blanco) to aged and smooth (añejo).
Rum — Made from sugarcane or molasses, often associated with tropical flavors. Can be light and mixable or dark and sipping-worthy.
Vodka — Neutral spirit that's clean and versatile, great for cocktails.
Gin — Flavored with botanicals (especially juniper), giving it herbal and floral notes.
Which of these sounds most appealing to you, or would you like recommendations based on flavor preferences (sweet, smoky, spicy, smooth)?

Great question! The good news is you probably already have most of what you need at home. Here's what helps when you're starting out:
What you'll need:
A glass — Any short glass works fine to start. You don't need fancy whiskey glasses yet.
Water — Keep spring water or soft tap water handy. Adding a bit of water can "open up" the spirit and help you detect finer notes, plus it takes the edge off the alcohol. Alternate sips of water and whisky to clear your palate.
Ice (optional) — If you want to try it "on the rocks," use big ice cubes or spheres that melt slower and won't water it down as much. Or skip ice entirely if you want to really taste the whisky.
Snacks (optional) — Unflavored, unsalted crackers or small slices of bread help cleanse your palate between sips, especially if you're trying multiple spirits.
How to drink it as a beginner:
Neat (straight) — Best for tasting the full flavor
On the rocks (over ice) — Refreshing and easier to acclimatize yourself to whisky
With a splash of water — Opens up the flavors and makes it smoother

How do I use it properly the very first time?
• Just now
Seen • Just now
Perfect question! Here's exactly how to taste whisky like a pro your very first time:
Step 1: Smell it first (The Aroma)
Gently bring the glass up to your nose — don't rush! You don't want to overwhelm your nose. Some people even nose spirits with one nostril first, then both. Take your nose away from the glass after each sniff, trust the first thing you smell, then repeat and other layers will reveal themselves. Try to name familiar smells — this takes practice!
Step 2: Take a small sip (The Taste)
Take a small sip and roll the spirit over your tongue and around its sides, then throughout your mouth. Savor the flavors and start identifying them — are they weak or strong? Herbal? Woody? Fruity? Spicy? Notice the texture and intensity too.
Step 3: Try it three ways
First sip: Neat (straight) to taste the full character
Second sip: Add a tiny splash of water — this "opens up" the flavors
Third sip: Try it on ice if you find it too strong
Pro tips:
Have water handy to alternate sips and clear your palate
Don't worry if you can't identify every flavor at first — it takes practice!
